newsitem.title: ITALY: Virgin to complain to EU over SAS fare tactics.
newsitem.headline: Virgin to complain to EU over SAS fare tactics.

text.p: European cut-price airline Virgin Express said on Monday it would complain to the European Commission over new tariffs introduced by the Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS).

Virgin Express chief executive Jonathan Ornstein told Reuters in an interview that SAS had cut the cost of tickets on its Brussels-Copenhagen route, but only for those flights which directly coincided with the cheap Virgin flights.
"We'll file a complaint to the (European) Commission to complain about this," he said.
Virgin owner, British entrepreneur Richard Branson, said he expected the commission would be sympathetic to their complaint.
"My guess is we'll be able to do something about this...the European Union has very strong laws," he told Reuters. SAS were not immediately available for comment.
Branson and Ornstein were in Italy to launch a new daily Virgin Express flight between Madrid and Rome.

Ornstein said the company's ticket prices were between 50 and 85 percent less than those offered by traditional national flag carriers, but added that the firm was already profitable, saying he expected it to have turnover of more than $200 million this year and profits of more than $10 million.

Branson launched the Brussels-based regional airline in April after buying 90 percent of EuroBelgian Airlines SA (EBA). The company forms part of the private Virgin group, which includes Virgin Atlantic Airways and package holiday and cargo affiliates in the Virgin Travel Group.

Virgin Express last month called off plans for a new Brussels-Geneva service after Swiss authorities objected to Virgin proposals to undercut by 50 percent the fares of Swissair and its Belgian affiliate Sabena.
Branson said the European Commission was so keen to boost competitivity in the air travel sector that they had phoned him to offer their help in his battle with the Swiss authorities.

"Virgin Express is the first major example the European Union can point to and say 'look at the benefits' (of market liberalisation)," he said. "I'd be surprised if we didn't get quick action against anti-competitive behaviour," he added. -- Crispian Balmer, Rome newsroom +396 6782501
